"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said Sept. 17.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Supreme Court allows Trump’s ‘third country’ deportation policy
summary: This is the second time the court has rejected lower court rulings that immigrants must be able to object before being sent to countries to which they have no previous connection.
story: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Tuesday removed obstacles to the Trump administration deporting certain immigrants to “third countries” where they have no connections.

The justices, with the court’s three liberals dissenting, granted an emergency request filed by the government seeking to block an appeals court ruling that said the current process is unlawful because the affected people are not given a proper chance to raise concerns about safety risks in violation of federal immigration law.
In the brief unsigned order, the court also said it would hear oral arguments in December and issue a definitive ruling on the legal questions raised in the litigation.

“A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike. It’s not too late to get $3,000 and a flight home,” James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, said in a statement Tuesday afternoon.

The Supreme Court last year allowed the policy to move forward after it was blocked by lower courts at an earlier stage of the litigation. It also later clarified its decision, at the request of the Trump administration, making it clear it applied to eight men the government wanted to send to South Sudan.
Since Trump’s second term began in January 2025, thousands of people have been sent to third countries, including South Sudan, Eswatini and Rwanda.
About 15,000 people were deported to third countries in 2025, according to the Migration Policy Institute, with Mexico receiving the majority.

The Supreme Court action “means that people facing removal to third countries are once again at immediate risk of being sent to places where they have no meaningful opportunity to seek protection,” said Trina Realmuto, a lawyer at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance representing plaintiffs. “That is an enormous consequence for people whose lives and safety are on the line.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Four unnamed immigrants challenged the policy, arguing that people should have a “meaningful opportunity” to claim that they could face torture or persecution if deported to one of the third countries.
Massachusetts-based U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy agreed. (It was his earlier ruling that the Supreme Court blocked last year, which led to heavy criticism from within MAGA world.)

The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Murphy’s most recent ruling and sided with the unnamed immigrants, citing a federal law that prevents deportations to a country where the person faces likely persecution.
Although the appeals court ruling was initially put on hold, on Sept. 23 it went into effect, prompting the Trump administration to rush to the Supreme Court.

In a court filing, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that putting “third country” deportations on hold “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations” and has “led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals.”
One scheduled flight that was to carry 70 people with criminal convictions to three different countries in the last week was immediately canceled, Sauer said.
The Trump administration has said no individualized determination is needed because the countries it has made deals with to take immigrants have said they would not mistreat them.
The government has said it would not immediately deport people if it has not received assurances from the country in question that people will not be tortured or persecuted.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs in court papers pointed out that the lower court rulings do not require anyone to be released from detention or even prevent third country removals if people are given a chance to raise objections.

The lead plaintiff, named only as D.V.D. in court records, is from Cuba and suffers from severe mental illness. He fears being sent to a country where he would not receive psychiatric treatment, the lawyers said.
People who have been deported to third countries have been mistreated, with some detained indefinitely and others subjected to physical and sexual abuse, the plaintiffs allege in court documents.

title: Pro-Trump TV ads paid for with Customs and Border Protection money, official says
summary: President Donald Trump’s administration paid for TV ads showing him in a favorable light using money intended for U.S.
story: President Donald Trump’s administration paid for TV ads showing him in a favorable light using money intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, an official and a top Republican senator confirmed to NBC News.
The source of the funding for the controversial ads the White House has described as public service announcements was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees CBP, referred requests for comment to the White House, which did not immediately respond.

The unusual ads — one of which is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — include disclaimers stating they were paid for by the U.S. government. The administration’s apparent use of taxpayer money to produce ads that resemble campaign advertisements has drawn bipartisan criticism.
“It’s a great message. I like the message,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Monday of the most recent ad, “but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Monday only Trump would have “the audacity to force Americans not only to watch his propaganda, but to pay for it.”

Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, confirmed the official’s account of the source of the funds, saying that “it was taken out of funding that was supposed to be for Customs and Border Protection” in Trump’s so-called big, beautiful bill, which Republicans passed along party lines in 2025.
For Subscribers

Collins, who faces a difficult re-election bid this fall, said the Appropriations Committee she chairs had no role in the money that the White House used. In fact, she said appropriations bills to fund the government typically have restrictions against using one account for another purpose.
“That’s why the administration went around the appropriations process and used an account that was part of the reconciliation bill,” Collins said in the Capitol.

The first of the ads aired earlier this month and featured Trump describing how he wanted to “defeat communism,” set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN. (Lawyers for JMSN on Monday sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House telling it to stop using his music.)
For Subscribers

The second spot closely tracks a 2024 Trump presidential campaign ad. It shows Trump walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voiceover to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”
The political ad-tracking firm AdImpact has estimated that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run the ads.
Earlier in Trump’s term, DHS used taxpayer money to run a series of ads featuring then-Secretary Kristi Noem encouraging immigrants living in the United States illegally to self-deport.
Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., who provided a key vote to pass the megabill, cast doubt on the wisdom of Trump’s decision when asked if pulling the money from CBP was a good move.

“Well, if that’s exactly what happened, probably not,” Justice said, while adding that he’s not an expert on the legality of the move. “But at the same time, I don’t know the particulars to say, well, that those dollars can be used that way, or they can’t be used that way. I don’t know. I just don’t know.”

“I can’t imagine how smart the people in the administration are that they’ve done something that’s just going to fly right in their face,” Justice said. “I can’t imagine that they’ve done something that they know is not right, not ethical, not whatever. I just couldn’t imagine they’d do that. They’re too smart for that.”
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who announced his retirement last year after clashing with Trump on the megabill, tore into the president’s decision to fund those ads with taxpayer money.

“I hate it. I tell you, it feels like Viktor Orbán talking to the Hungarian people. There’s no place for that sort of thing,” Tillis said, while adding that Trump could have used political resources if he wanted to run a political ad. “If it were, you know, some clear message that was going to appeal to the broader, a real public service announcement, that’s fine. But that was not that.”

title: Trump’s border wall construction cut into an ancient ground carving older than Stonehenge
summary: The Las Playas intaglio carving of a huge fish is  at least two thousand  years older than the first Egyptian pyramid, according to researchers’ recent estimations.
story: An ancient ground carving that was severely damaged by the administration’s border wall construction was created before Stonehenge and Egypt’s oldest pyramid, according to recently publicized research.

The Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish carved into the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, is now considered the oldest example in the Americas of a geoglyphic, the ancient art form that is carved into or drawn on the ground.

In April, contractors hired by the Trump administration to make way for a second wall along the Arizona-Mexico border “scraped” a 50-foot swath through the ancient carving, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, which documented the damage.

The intaglio on the ground of the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous tribes is estimated to be about 2,000 years older than Egypt’s first pyramid and to have been created about 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge and 4,000 years before Peru’s Nazca Lines, researchers have found.

The formerly 272-foot carving had originally been thought to be about 1,000 years old. But the latest research dates the art’s creation to at least 6,500 years ago, and possibly as much as 7,500 years ago.
That age emphasizes “the significance of this site and the parallel great misfortune resulting from its damage,” the researchers said in an article published in The SAA Archaeological Record.

“This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It’s a cultural and historical atrocity,” Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement.

A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in an email to NBC News that the contractor “inadvertently disturbed” the site and that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has been “engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“The remaining portion of the site has been secured and will be protected in place. CBP is conducting a thorough review of construction protocols and strengthening communication procedures to ensure this does not happen again,” the spokesperson stated, adding that the agency is “committed to respecting and safeguarding cultural heritage throughout all border infrastructure projects.”

The damage to that site and construction on other parts of Tohono O’odham land and sacred Indigenous areas has strained the tenuous relationship between the tribal nation and the government. The tribe is appealing a federal judge’s decision refusing to block the administration’s border wall construction through its reservation.

While the intaglio’s site is irreparably damaged, the Tohono O’odham people are trying to stop the government from plowing through Quitobaquito Springs, a desert water source in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument that is also considered a sacred site and holds endangered species.

In order to build the border wall and barriers, the Department of Homeland Security invoked authority granted in the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to waive numerous laws protecting the environment, water, cultural, historical and religious sites.

The Tohono O’odham Nation has long worked with CBP, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, on border security, helping to keep drug traffickers and others from using its land for criminal activity.

The tribe’s reservation straddles the U.S.-Mexico border, and its members have permission to move between the two countries with ID checks. About 3,000 of its members are in Mexico, according to the tribal nation.

The Center for Biological Diversity stated in a news release that conservation advocates and tribal nations have long warned that border wall and secondary border barrier plans could cut through sensitive habitat and cultural sites across the region.
Wall construction in other parts of the border has sparked other lawsuits and opposition from landowners, Native American tribes, local governments, conservation groups, business owners and others.

In Texas, a tribal nonprofit for the Lipan Apache and an outdoor recreation business have opposed the border wall construction, alleging DHS is not authorized to violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which they say it would do by destroying or cutting off access to sacred sites.

A federal judge ordered a temporary halt to construction in Big Bend National Park in response to the lawsuit, but construction continues on other parts of the rugged, undeveloped and remote region outside state and federal parkland.

title: Caleb Flynn, former ‘American Idol’ singer, found guilty of wife’s murder
summary: Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty Tuesday of murdering his wife in their Ohio home in February.
story: Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty Tuesday of murdering his wife in their Ohio home in February.
The jury took a little over two hours to convict Flynn on all nine counts of murder, assault and tampering with evidence in the death of Ashley Flynn, 37.

After Judge Jeannine Pratt read the verdict in Miami County Court of Common Pleas in Troy, Flynn broke down in tears and repeatedly wiped his nose and eyes. He was taken from the courtroom in handcuffs.
Following the proceedings, Miami County Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins read from a statement released by Ashley’s family, who said the verdict brings “justice and accountability.”

“However,” he continued, reading from the statement, “no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their mother, or erase the pain our family has endured. The cruelty of what happened to Ashley, and the things we’ve been forced to hear and relive, have at times felt unbearable.”
Sentencing will be Oct. 5, when Flynn faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Defense attorney Patrick Mulligan said his client will challenge the verdict.
“This decision will be tested thoroughly in the Court of Appeals,” Mulligan said after Tuesday’s proceedings.
Caleb Flynn found guilty of wife's murder

Flynn, a former music pastor, told a 911 dispatcher that his wife, who worked as a schoolteacher and volleyball coach, had been shot multiple times in the head by an intruder. He told the dispatcher that he did not know whether the intruder was still in their Tipp City home.

In police interviews played in court, Flynn told officers that he was sleeping on the couch when he woke up to the sound of gunshots. He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.”

When police arrived at the home on the day of the shooting, the garage door, a side door and the center console of Flynn’s pickup truck were open. Flynn told police that he kept a gun in the console, but no weapon was found there.

Prosecutors alleged that Flynn, 40, staged the home invasion to mislead investigators and shared thoughts of killing his wife in text messages to his then-mistress. Authorities never found the gun used in the killing.
Add to Google
Add to Google
“The evidence has proven the defendant’s account to be a complete fabrication,” Assistant Prosecuting Attorney Matthew C. Joseph said in closings Tuesday.

“While the defendant told law enforcement that he was sleeping, his electronic devices documented something different. They documented movement and activity in the hours leading up to Ashley’s murder,” Joseph said. “The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving.”

Joseph told the court that Flynn, who sang in televised auditions in Chicago for Season 12 of “American Idol” in 2013 but did not advance to the main competition, “wanted to be a victim” and wanted to “keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself.”

“Being the victim allowed him to do that without being the husband who left his wife for a mistress,” Joseph said. “Instead, he’d be the husband whose wife was tragically murdered by an unknown intruder.”

Over eight days, the jury heard from 40 prosecution witnesses, including Alleigha Botner, who said she met Flynn when she was 20 and an intern at his church. She said they had been having an affair at the time of Ashley’s killing.

Botner, now 24, testified that Flynn had made remarks that he hated his wife and harbored thoughts of killing her. Botner sobbed on the stand as she read some of their text messages, telling the court that she regretted having told him in one message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.”
In other text messages shown in court, Flynn discussed wanting his wife dead.

“I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail,” he is alleged to have written in a text in August 2025, about six months before the killing.
Add to Google
Add to Google

In another text, Botner said she wasn’t serious. “I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.”
Botner told the court that her feelings about Flynn have since changed and that she hated him. When a prosecutor asked her why, she said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.”
The defense rested Monday without calling a single witness.
Mulligan, one of Flynn’s defense attorneys, said in his closing argument that being “unfaithful doesn’t equal murder.”
“This case is wholly lacking in concrete evidence. Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn’t solve the case,” he said.
Afterward, Mulligan said the defense was “disappointed” in the jury’s decision.
Ashley’s family said she lived a virtuous life.

“She loved being a mom,” Watkins said, still reading from the family statement. “She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy and grace. We refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley’s life have the final word in her story.”
Watkins praised law enforcement and prosecutors for their success in prosecuting the case. He said he is tired of talking about Flynn and wants renewed focus on the victim.
“This world would be a much better place if all of us in it lived like Ashley,” he said.

title: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman is evicted from her home of 70 years
summary: An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
story: An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.

Supporters had gathered outside her building overnight on Friday, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.

The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to fierce public anger.

On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction, some setting off flares. They carried placards reading “Not one more eviction, not one less neighbor, we are all Maricarmen” and “right to housing at a fair price.”

At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza, some pitching tents. They remained in place early Sunday as dozens of activists staged a sit-in. A model of a vulture, decrying so-called vulture funds, hung above the camp.
Earlier in the week, tenants unions and other housing groups held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.

Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.

“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”
Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.

“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.
Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.

The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.
The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.

Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she was worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.
“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”

Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said that she was looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.

“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”
Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.
“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.

It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”
“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”

title: OpenAI launches always-on AI agents a day after apologizing for a hack by its bots
summary: OpenAI announced its new AI agent product, Dots, amid a barrage of controversy over AI agents that had gone rogue.
story: SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants.

Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons.
CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users.

“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said.

OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive.
Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties.

Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work.

title: Venezuelan man shot and wounded by ICE agent in Texas is charged with assaulting an officer
summary: Garcés Pérez was wounded by an ICE officer on Sept. 20 while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries; his attorneys say a bullet lodged in his spine is causing “grave danger.”
story: Federal prosecutors in Texas announced charges on Tuesday against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan delivery drivershot and seriously wounded by an ICE officer in Austin earlier this month. The charges came a day before he was set to appear in court to challenge the legality of his immigration detention.

Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.

Garcés Pérez was wounded by an ICE officer in the upper part of his back on Sept. 20 while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries. His attorneys say the bullet is still lodged near his spine, causing “grave danger.” A Democratic congressman who visited Garcés last week said he was in a wheelchair, in pain and in need of surgery.
“We are all laser-focused on making sure that Wilber doesn’t die in custody,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the legal nonprofit Texas Civil Rights Project who is part of Garcés’ legal team.
Garcés Pérez had his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday, said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons in a statement.

The criminal complaint accuses Garcés Pérez of striking an ICE officer’s torso with his car’s side mirror while trying to drive away. This officer was not wearing a body camera at the time of the encounter, as the Department of Homeland Security has stated previously, but the complaint includes images appearing to capture this moment from the body camera of a second ICE officer who was also there. After this, “a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area” ensued, the complaint states.
Tuesday’s court appearance following the criminal complaint took Garcés Pérez’s legal team “as a surprise,” they told NBC News in a statement.

“His attorneys only learned of this appearance due to a pre-scheduled meeting they had with him this morning, in which he did not appear,” their statement said. “This morning, when his attorneys were finally able to see him, he was in considerable pain, dizzy, and needed pain medication, which had not been provided. Rather than provide the life saving medical care he needs, DHS and the government are playing games with his life.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Garcés Pérez was transferred out of a facility in San Antonio, where he had been in immigration custody for nine days, and placed in federal criminal custody in a facility near Austin, according to Garza.
“It has created a web of detention for him,” she said of having Garcés Pérez be transferred from custody.

According to the complaint, after the chase began, the ICE officer wearing his body camera — identified in the complaint by the initials D.F. — lost sight of Garcés Pérez and of the other ICE officer, who was not wearing his body camera and is identified in the complaint by the initials L.G.

The ICE officer who was not wearing his body camera eventually called his colleague. “L.G. told D.F. that Garcs had attempted to strike L.G. with his car and L.G. had fired his pistol,” the complaint states. The complaint provides no visual evidence of that interaction.

The complaint also includes the account of events Garcés Pérez provided to federal investigators. He said an SUV from one of the ICE officers struck his “car and caused it to spin around” following a short pursuit, the complaint states. “After coming to a forced stop, Garces recalled L.G. firing his pistol into the backright window of Garces’ car. Garces was struck with a bullet in his upper back.”
By contrast, U.S. Attorney Simmons said in the statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol.”
The court hearing scheduled for Wednesday in Garcés Pérez’s lawsuit challenging his detention was canceled.
Last Tuesday, a federal judge had granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to one of his attorneys, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.
“We are still fighting to ensure that the government doesn’t re detain him under immigration custody following whatever is being done on the criminal side,” Garza said.

title: Toddler takes loaded gun to Michigan daycare
summary: Daycare staff members took the gun from the toddler and no one was hurt Monday in Canton Township, a community west of Detroit, police said.
story: Police took a parent into custody this week after a toddler at a Michigan daycare center pulled a loaded handgun in a holster from their backpack, police said.
No one was hurt in the incident Monday in Canton Township, and Police Chief Joseph Bialy praised daycare staff members for their handling of the situation.
“I’ve watched the video. I’ve seen what their staff did,” he said at a news conference Monday. “And they were prepared and ready to be able to remove this firearm and keep all the kids safe.”
Police did not identify the parents, and no criminal charges had been filed by Tuesday afternoon.

One of the parents is a law enforcement officer in a neighboring jurisdiction, Bialy said. That was not the parent who was taken into custody, he said. He did not believe the weapon was a service weapon.
The firearm — a handgun that was in a holster — came into the building in a backpack, Bialy said.
The incident was captured on video that shows the toddler removing the firearm from the backpack, Bialy said.
“It’s shocking to see,” he said.
A teacher was in the room the entire time, saw what was happening and took swift action to intervene, Bialy said.
“Had that not happened, I do not know where we would be right now or what kind of conversation we would be having,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The daycare center has disenrolled the family, NBC affiliate WDIV of Detroit reported.
The facility where the incident occurred, Childrens World Early Learning Center, said it would also start searching backpacks entering the building.
“We remain committed to ensuring our center is a safe haven for every child and family we serve,” it said.
The Wayne County Prosecutor’s Office said Tuesday afternoon that a warrant request was being reviewed but that there would be no arraignment that day.
Bialy called the situation a serious incident and said police were treating it that way. He stressed the importance of safe storage of firearms.
“I don’t think there was any ill intent by truly anyone involved,” Bialy said. “I think it really falls back on safe security of a firearm.”
“The law is clear”: If a child is present or expected to be present, firearms must be secured, he said.

title: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
summary: Sean “Diddy” Combs has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to a low-security correctional facility in southern New Jersey, sources said.
story: Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.

This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison

Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.

Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.

“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”

“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.

He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.

Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”

Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem. Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.

Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof. The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.

Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter.
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.

Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.

Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.

His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July. He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”

title: People with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 60 pounds on Lilly’s latest weight loss drug
summary: Participants who took the experimental drug retatrutide experienced the largest weight loss ever seen in a drug trial for diabetes.
story: Eli Lilly’s highly anticipated GLP-1 drug retatrutide helped people with Type 2 diabetes lose up to 60 pounds, or about 23% of their body weight, according to late-stage trial results published Tuesday in The Lancet.
It’s the most weight loss ever recorded in a drug trial for diabetes patients, a group that often has a harder time losing weight.

In clinical trials for semaglutide and tirzepatide, people with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 10% (21 pounds) and 15% (34 pounds) of their body weight, respectively. (Those are not direct comparisons, as the drugs were not evaluated in head-to-head clinical trials.)

Retatrutide “is truly an advance in diabetes care,” said Dr. Susan Spratt, an endocrinologist and the senior medical director for the Population Health Management Office at Duke Health in North Carolina. She was not involved in the trial and does not receive money from Eli Lilly. “It rivals gastric bypass surgery without the surgery.”
Spratt said many diabetes medications, such as insulin, cause weight gain.
“It can be discouraging to manage your diabetes well but gain weight,” she said.

Lilly’s trial included more than 1,110 patients who had an average starting weight of about 234 pounds and an average body mass index, or BMI, of about 38. People were randomly assigned to take one of three weekly doses of retatrutide or a placebo for 80 weeks. By the end of the trial, more than half of participants’ BMI fell below 30, the cutoff for obesity.

Results from another trial, published Tuesday in the New England Journal of Medicine, found retatrutide helped patients without Type 2 diabetes who have obesity or are overweight lose up to 70 pounds, or 25% of their body weight on average, after 80 weeks. That data included a subset of patients with severe obesity, who lost up to 85 pounds, or 30% of their body weight, after 104 weeks — the most weight loss ever recorded in a medication trial and on par with bariatric surgery.

Like semaglutide and tirzepatide, retatrutide works by mimicking a hormone called GLP-1. What sets retatrutide apart is its classification as a “triple agonist.” Lilly’s tirzepatide, a “double agonist,” mimics two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP), and retatrutide targets three by adding a hormone called glucagon.

Lilly hasn’t submitted retatrutide for approval to the Food and Drug Administration, but its clinical trial results have already cemented it as one of the drug industry’s most highly anticipated treatments. Lilly says it plans to file for approval early next year.

Unauthorized, copycat versions of retatrutide are already being made and sold through wellness platforms, med spas and compounding pharmacies. The drug is often labeled as “for research use only,” a legal workaround to sell compounds they claim aren’t meant for humans. Lilly has filed lawsuits against companies selling unapproved versions of the drug.
Retatrutide’s other benefits
Retatrutide also helps reduce the severity of sleep apnea and lower knee arthritis pain. Earlier data suggests the drug appears to help the heart.
For Subscribers
The new trial found that retatrutide, like other GLP-1 drugs, which were initially developed as diabetes medications, effectively lowered blood sugar levels in patients with diabetes.
For Subscribers

Retatrutide lowered A1C levels — a measure of a person’s average blood sugar levels over the previous two to three months — by up to 1.6%, compared with 0.2% with a placebo, according to the trial results.
Up to 40% of patients in the trial reached an A1C below 5.7%, below the cutoff for diabetes and prediabetes.

“The retatrutide data is very exciting,” Dr. Michelle Ponder, an assistant professor of medicine at Duke University School of Medicine in North Carolina, wrote in an email. A 5.7% A1C level means “that their diabetes went into remission,” said Ponder, who was not involved with Lilly’s trial.
She added, however, that retatrutide “may be too strong for some patients,” particularly those with only mild diabetes or slightly elevated weight.
They “may be better suited to the medications we already have available on the market such as Ozempic or Mounjaro,” she said.
She added that whenever switching medications, there is a chance patients could experience a change in the frequency of side effects.

Side effects of retatrutide were similar to those of other GLP-1 medications, with patients most commonly reporting diarrhea, nausea, constipation and vomiting. Lilly said the side effects were mild to moderate in severity. About 8% of people in the trial taking the highest dose stopped taking the drug, compared with about 5% of people taking the placebo.

title: Another majority that could be in Democrats’ reach: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we take stock of how the gubernatorial landscape is shaping up across the country. Plus, Scott Wong and Monica Alba recap President Donald Trump’s much-anticipated lunch with AI industry leaders.
— Adam Wollner
Another majority that could be in Democrats’ reach

Five weeks out from Election Day, Democrats increasingly have their sights set on not only winning control of the House, but the Senate, too, as the political environment continues to deteriorate for the GOP.
That environment could also present Democrats with an opening outside of Washington to achieve something they haven’t done in 16 years: hold a majority of the country’s governorships.

Currently, there are 26 governors who are Republicans and 24 who are Democrats. Thirty-six states are holding gubernatorial elections this fall, with an even split of Democratic- and Republican-held seats on the ballot.
So Democrats need to flip a net of two governorships for a majority. But similar to the battle for the Senate, their path involves winning in decidedly red territory.

For starters, Democrats are defending a seat in Kansas, a state President Donald Trump won by 16 points in 2024. With Gov. Laura Kelly term-limited, Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson will face off against state Sen. Cindy Holscher, who defeated a more moderate opponent in last month’s Democratic primary.

Democrats are also defending governorships in the key swing states of Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Michigan and Wisconsin are open-seat races, while Gov. Katie Hobbs is running for a second term in Arizona after narrowly winning her first by 17,000 votes four years ago. For his part, Gov. Josh Shapiro has enjoyed strong approval ratings in Pennsylvania and is a heavy favorite there.

Assuming they hold all, or at least most, of those governorships, there is a growing number of opportunities for Democrats to pick up the two (or more) they’d need for a majority in states Trump carried.

According to new race ratings from the NBC News Decision Desk, the Iowa governor’s contest is listed as “lean Democrat.” Democratic state Auditor Rob Stand has established a moderate brand in the state as he faces businessman Zach Lahn, who has aligned himself with the “Make America Healthy Again” movement.

Meanwhile, three other seats Republicans are defending — in Georgia, Nevada and Ohio — are rated as “toss-ups.” In Alaska, Democrats are feeling better about their chances after one of their candidates advanced from the all-party primary to face three Republicans on the ranked choice general election ballot. And in Texas, Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa is running more competitively than expected against GOP Gov. Greg Abbott.

While state races are often less affected by the national political winds than those at the federal level (just look at deep-blue Vermont, where Republican Gov. Phil Scott is still considered the favorite), they can still prove difficult for any candidate of the party in power in Washington to overcome at a certain point.
For Subscribers

Securing a majority of governorships nationwide is more symbolic compared with the power that comes with House or Senate control. But it would still represent a significant moral victory for Democrats, given the recent string of Republican dominance at the state level. Aside from a brief period in which Democrats controlled a majority of governors’ seats from the 2006 to the 2010 elections, Republicans have otherwise held that distinction since the 1994 elections.
For Subscribers

And it would help Democrats fight against their coastal image and prove they can win in places all across the country, as they figure out what course they want to chart heading into the 2028 presidential campaign.
💰Related: Democrats face a staggering spending disadvantage in Georgia’s tight race for governor, by Adam Edelman
After summit with tech titans, Trump calls for ‘tremendous self-regulation’ by AI companies

After privately huddling with nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch today, President Donald Trump continued to push back on calls for new safety regulations for artificial intelligence, saying there was agreement in the room that there should be “tremendous self-regulation” by companies.

“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that,” said Trump, flanked by tech and government leaders.

The gathering Tuesday included a who’s who of the tech world, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and OpenAI President Greg Brockman.

Trump hosted the lunch with House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles also attended.

Trump also addressed the proliferation of data centers, which are unpopular among voters but are being built to power AI companies. The president, who supports data centers, said tech leaders will work with local communities and help pay for things like energy and education.

“This is a group that loves local communities. They love our country, and they’re going to work with local communities for the data centers, in particular, and they’re going to work to make the community happy,” Trump told reporters. “That might be supplying oil and gas. It might be supplying education. It may be helping teachers along financially. ... So you’re going to see data centers are going to be very popular.”
Trump said he planned to sign a document later in the day to rename artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.”
Earlier, Trump unveiled America.gov, a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a “one-stop shop” for Americans navigating government services.
